newsitem.title: USA: R.J. Reynolds sues FTC over Joe Camel action.
newsitem.headline: R.J. Reynolds sues FTC over Joe Camel action.

text.p: R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. struck back at the Federal Trade Commission on Tuesday with a lawsuit that seeks to block the FTC's crackdown on Joe Camel, the tobacco company's controversial marketing symbol.
The nation's No. 2 cigarette maker filed the suit in U.S. District Court in North Carolina, alleging the agency violated the law and even its own statutes to shut down the advertising campaign.

"We have asked the court to review the facts...which clearly demonstrate an agency engaged in harassment and political interference in a fair process," R.J. Reynolds said in a statement issued late Tuesday.
Reynolds Tobacco is 80.5-percent owned by RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.

Joe Camel, a cartoon caricature of a camel that wears black leather jackets, plays billiards and looks debonair with a cigarette in his snout, brought a resurgence to the Camel brand of cigarettes when introduced in 1988.
But it brought along an avalanche of criticism from the health community and others who excoriated the campaign for allegedly targeting children -- not just teenagers, but little children.
The FTC voted May 28 to issue a complaint against the Joe Camel campaign, reopening a probe that had closed in 1994 after the agency determined there was no basis to file a complaint.

Reynolds, in its statement Tuesday, said there has been a 75-percent drop in underage smoker interest in the cartoon since 1994, but that the commission issued its newest complaint before data showing the decline could be distributed.
The FTC's latest complaint cited the "unfair" aspects of the advertising.

"We allege that this is an unfair advertising campaign, in that it targeted consumers who were not legally able to buy the product. We're alleging that they targeted a campaign to an underage consuming population," said Victoria Streitfeld, a spokesperson for the FTC, in telephone interview Wednesday.
"The commission has reason to believe that RJR has violated a law. We will present our evidence before an administrative law judge," she said.
In its suit, R.J. Reynolds asked the court to order the FTC to close the renewed investigation, withdraw its complaint and "be enjoined from future violations of laws and procedure."
RJR's stock fell 75 cents to $34.375 on the New York Stock Exchange at mid-aftrernoon.
